claim: ESCRT pathways drive many important cellular membrane fission reactions.
source: Many important cellular membrane fission reactions are driven by ESCRT pathways, which culminate in disassembly of ESCRT-III polymers by the AAA ATPase Vps4.
evidence: This is a general statement about ESCRT pathways supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: ESCRT pathways culminate in disassembly of ESCRT-III polymers by the AAA ATPase Vps4.
source: Many important cellular membrane fission reactions are driven by ESCRT pathways, which culminate in disassembly of ESCRT-III polymers by the AAA ATPase Vps4.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the active Vps4 hexamer with its cofactor Vta1, ADP·BeFx, and an ESCRT-III substrate peptide was determined at 4.3 Å resolution.
source: We report a 4.3 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the active Vps4 hexamer with its cofactor Vta1, ADP·BeFx, and an ESCRT-III substrate peptide.
evidence: The resolution is reported in the abstract and supported by structural data presented in the manuscript including FSC curves and refinement statistics.

claim: Four Vps4 subunits form a helix whose interfaces are consistent with ATP binding.
source: Four Vps4 subunits form a helix whose interfaces are consistent with ATP binding, is stabilized by Vta1, and binds the substrate peptide.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing the arrangement of subunits A-D and their nucleotide-binding sites.

claim: The four-subunit Vps4 helix is stabilized by Vta1.
source: Four Vps4 subunits form a helix whose interfaces are consistent with ATP binding, is stabilized by Vta1, and binds the substrate peptide.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing Vta1 binding between adjacent Vps4 subunits and biochemical data showing enhanced binding affinity.

claim: The four-subunit Vps4 helix binds the substrate peptide.
source: Four Vps4 subunits form a helix whose interfaces are consistent with ATP binding, is stabilized by Vta1, and binds the substrate peptide.
evidence: This is supported by density for the peptide in the cryo-EM structure and fluorescence polarization binding data.

claim: The fifth Vps4 subunit approximately continues the helix but appears to be dissociating.
source: The fifth subunit approximately continues this helix but appears to be dissociating.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis showing the D-E interface has an expanded nucleotide-binding site and altered geometry compared to the A-B, B-C, and C-D interfaces.

claim: The final Vps4 subunit completes a notched-washer configuration as if transitioning between the ends of the helix.
source: The final Vps4 subunit completes a notched-washer configuration as if transitioning between the ends of the helix.
evidence: This is based on structural data showing subunit F in multiple positions that appear to connect the end and beginning of the helix.

claim: ATP binding propagates growth at one end of the Vps4 helix.
source: We propose that ATP binding propagates growth at one end of the helix while hydrolysis promotes disassembly at the other end, so that Vps4 'walks' along ESCRT-III until it encounters the ordered N-terminal domain to destabilize the ESCRT-III lattice.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data showing different nucleotide states at different interfaces.

claim: ATP hydrolysis promotes disassembly at the other end of the Vps4 helix.
source: We propose that ATP binding propagates growth at one end of the helix while hydrolysis promotes disassembly at the other end, so that Vps4 'walks' along ESCRT-III until it encounters the ordered N-terminal domain to destabilize the ESCRT-III lattice.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data showing different nucleotide states at different interfaces.

claim: Vps4 'walks' along ESCRT-III until it encounters the ordered N-terminal domain to destabilize the ESCRT-III lattice.
source: We propose that ATP binding propagates growth at one end of the helix while hydrolysis promotes disassembly at the other end, so that Vps4 'walks' along ESCRT-III until it encounters the ordered N-terminal domain to destabilize the ESCRT-III lattice.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data and previous knowledge about ESCRT-III structure.

claim: The proposed Vps4 mechanism may be generally applicable to other protein-translocating AAA ATPases.
source: This model may be generally applicable to other protein-translocating AAA ATPases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on structural similarities between Vps4 and other AAA ATPases discussed in the manuscript.

claim: ESCRT pathways mediate membrane deformation and fission in cytokinetic abscission.
source: These include membrane severing during cytokinetic abscission, the formation of multivesicular bodies and exosomes, shedding of microvesicles and viruses, repair of lesions in the plasma membrane, pruning of neurons, removal of defective nuclear pore complex assembly intermediates, and nuclear envelope closure at mitotic exit (Campsteijn et al., 2016; Hurley, 2015; McCullough et al., 2013; Olmos and Carlton, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Seven ESCRT-III family members are recognized in yeast.
source: The ESCRT pathways converge on the recruitment of ESCRT-III subunits, of which seven family members are recognized in yeast and 12 in human.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Twelve ESCRT-III family members are recognized in human.

evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Upstream factors recruit ESCRT-III subunits, which polymerize through their N-terminal domains to induce an inherently unstable membrane configuration that resolves by fission following Vps4-mediated disassembly or remodeling of the ESCRT-III polymer.
source: The leading model is that the upstream factors recruit ESCRT-III subunits, which polymerize through their N-terminal domains to induce an inherently unstable membrane configuration that resolves by fission following Vps4-mediated disassembly or remodeling of the ESCRT-III polymer (Henne et al., 2013; McCullough et al., 2013; Schöneberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is described as the leading model and is supported by citations.

claim: The N-terminal MIT domain of Vps4 binds ~20 residue MIT interacting motifs (MIMs) that are found at the C-termini of many ESCRT-III subunits.
source: The N-terminal MIT domain of Vps4 (Scott et al., 2005b) binds ~20 residue MIT interacting motifs (MIMs) that are found at the C-termini of many ESCRT-III subunits (Kieffer et al., 2008; Obita et al., 2007; Stuchell-Brereton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The MIT domain is followed by a flexible ~40 residue linker.
source: The MIT domain is followed by a flexible ~40 residue linker and an ~320 residue AAA ATPase cassette that comprises a large AAA ATPase domain and a small AAA ATPase domain (Figures 1A and 2A), which contains an insertion known as the β domain that binds the dimeric C-terminal VSL domain of the Vta1 cofactor (LIP5 in human) in an interaction that promotes Vps4 assembly and ATPase activity (Azmi et al., 2006; Lottridge et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge and is illustrated in the figures.

claim: Vps4 is monomeric or dimeric in the cytosol.
source: Vps4 is monomeric or dimeric in the cytosol, and assembles to form an active hexamer upon concentration at the membrane/ESCRT-III surface (Monroe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Vps4 assembles to form an active hexamer upon concentration at the membrane/ESCRT-III surface.

claim: The central pore of the Vps4 hexamer is thought to be lined by pore loop 1 and pore loop 2.
source: The central pore of this hexamer is thought to be lined by pore loop 1 and pore loop 2 (residues 203–210 and 240–248, respectively), which are highly conserved in AAA ATPases that act on protein substrates and play a critical role in substrate translocation (Gonciarz et al., 2008; Han et al., 2015; Kieffer et al., 2008; Monroe and Hill, 2016; Scott et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is consistent with the structural data presented.

claim: Pore loop 1 and pore loop 2 play a critical role in substrate translocation.

claim: Nucleotide-induced asymmetry is required for binding of a peptide from an ESCRT-III subunit to the central pore of the Vps4 hexamer.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The 8-residue peptide DEIVNKVL (Vps2 residues 165–172) binds Vps4 with essentially the same ~200 nM KD as the 20-residue parent peptide.

evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 1A-B.

evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM structure showing asymmetry in Vps4.

source: This variation in the quality of Vta1VSL densities among the six interfaces likely reflects differences in occupancy and binding modes at each site, as discussed below.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variation in density quality.

claim: Y303 and Y310 of the first Vta1 subunit contact two loops of the β domain (residues 356–359 and 375–385).
source: In all cases, the Vta1VSL dimer contacts the β domain of one Vps4 subunit in an interface that we have modeled according to a previously reported crystal structure (Yang and Hurley, 2010) in which Y303 and Y310 of the first Vta1 subunit contact two loops of the β domain (residues 356–359 and 375–385) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on modeling according to a previous crystal structure and the current cryo-EM structure.

claim: The Vta1VSL construct in the current structure is extended by 10 residues at the N-terminus compared to the earlier crystal structure.
source: Compared to the earlier crystal structure, the Vta1VSL construct in our structure is extended by 10 residues at the N-terminus, including residues of the 'Vps4 stimulatory element' (Norgan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the constructs used in different studies.

claim: The N-terminal extension of Vta1VSL includes residues of the 'Vps4 stimulatory element'.
source: Compared to the earlier crystal structure, the Vta1VSL construct in our structure is extended by 10 residues at the N-terminus, including residues of the 'Vps4 stimulatory element' (Norgan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous work.

claim: The N-terminal residues of Vta1VSL make a small 70 Å2 contact with α7 and α9 in the small AAA ATPase domain of the same Vps4 subunit.
source: Some density for these residues is visible for the second subunit of the best-defined Vta1VSL dimers, where they make a small 70 Å2 contact with α7 and α9 in the small AAA ATPase domain of the same Vps4 subunit, as suggested previously (Davies et al., 2014) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and surface area calculations.

claim: Vta1VSL dimers bound to the β domains of subunits A, B, C, and F also contact the small AAA ATPase domain of the following Vps4 subunit.
source: Consistent with their more clearly defined density, the Vta1VSL dimers bound to the β domains of subunits A, B, C, and F also contact the small AAA ATPase domain of the following Vps4 subunit (Figure 4C), with Y310' and surrounding residues at the hairpin end of the second Vta1 subunit contacting α6 and α7 (residues 300–330) of the small AAA ATPase domain of the second Vps4.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Y310' and surrounding residues at the hairpin end of the second Vta1 subunit contact α6 and α7 (residues 300–330) of the small AAA ATPase domain of the second Vps4.
source: Consistent with their more clearly defined density, the Vta1VSL dimers bound to the β domains of subunits A, B, C, and F also contact the small AAA ATPase domain of the following Vps4 subunit (Figure 4C), with Y310' and surrounding residues at the hairpin end of the second Vta1 subunit contacting α6 and α7 (residues 300–330) of the small AAA ATPase domain of the second Vps4.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Vta1VSL dimer uses two-fold symmetry-related residues Y310 and Y310' to contact different surfaces on neighboring Vps4 subunits.
source: This novel interaction shows an unusual use of the two-fold symmetry-related VSL dimer residues, Y310 and Y310', to contact different surfaces on neighboring Vps4 subunits, which is consistent with our biochemical finding that Vta1 stabilizes formation of the hexamer (Monroe et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2005a) rather than higher-order assemblies (Xiao et al., 2008; Yang and Hurley, 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with biochemical data.

claim: Vta1 stabilizes formation of the Vps4 hexamer rather than higher-order assemblies.
source: This novel interaction shows an unusual use of the two-fold symmetry-related VSL dimer residues, Y310 and Y310', to contact different surfaces on neighboring Vps4 subunits, which is consistent with our biochemical finding that Vta1 stabilizes formation of the hexamer (Monroe et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2005a) rather than higher-order assemblies (Xiao et al., 2008; Yang and Hurley, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and biochemical data in the manuscript.

claim: Vta1VSL dimers can bind in the same manner to the Vps4 subunit pairs F-A, A-B, B-C, C-D.
source: Vta1VSL dimers can bind in the same manner to the Vps4 subunit pairs F-A, A-B, B-C, C-D, but interactions at the D-E and E-F subunit pairs appear to be suboptimal.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Interactions of Vta1VSL at the D-E and E-F subunit pairs appear to be suboptimal.
source: Vta1VSL dimers can bind in the same manner to the Vps4 subunit pairs F-A, A-B, B-C, C-D, but interactions at the D-E and E-F subunit pairs appear to be suboptimal.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The D-E and E-F interfaces are incompatible with Vta1 forming the same contacts between neighboring Vps4 subunits as seen at the A-B, B-C, C-D, and F-A interfaces.
source: In contrast, the D-E and E-F interfaces are incompatible with Vta1 forming the same contacts between neighboring Vps4 subunits as seen at the A-B, B-C, C-D, and F-A interfaces (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Vta1VSL at the D-E and E-F interfaces remains bound to the β domain of the first Vps4 subunit but cannot form optimal contacts with its adjacent subunit.
source: Instead, our preferred interpretation of the density is that Vta1VSL at the D-E and E-F interfaces remains bound to the β domain of the first Vps4 subunit but cannot form optimal contacts with its adjacent subunit.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the density and structural analysis.

claim: The Vps4101-437-Hcp1 hexamer shows an ~30 fold tighter apparent KD for Vta1VSL binding than Vps4101-437 L151D.
source: The Vps4101-437-Hcp1 hexamer showed an ~30 fold tighter apparent KD than Vps4101-437 L151D (Figure 5), which supports our observation that Vta1VSL binds to two neighboring Vps4 subunits in the hexamer and is consistent with a role for Vta1 in stabilizing assembly of the active Vta1 hexamer (Azmi et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence polarization binding data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The enhanced binding of Vta1VSL to the Vps4 hexamer supports the observation that Vta1VSL binds to two neighboring Vps4 subunits in the hexamer.
source: The Vps4101-437-Hcp1 hexamer showed an ~30 fold tighter apparent KD than Vps4101-437 L151D (Figure 5), which supports our observation that Vta1VSL binds to two neighboring Vps4 subunits in the hexamer and is consistent with a role for Vta1 in stabilizing assembly of the active Vta1 hexamer (Azmi et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is based on biochemical data and structural analysis.

claim: The enhanced binding of Vta1VSL to the Vps4 hexamer is consistent with a role for Vta1 in stabilizing assembly of the active Vps4 hexamer.
source: The Vps4101-437-Hcp1 hexamer showed an ~30 fold tighter apparent KD than Vps4101-437 L151D (Figure 5), which supports our observation that Vta1VSL binds to two neighboring Vps4 subunits in the hexamer and is consistent with a role for Vta1 in stabilizing assembly of the active Vta1 hexamer (Azmi et al., 2006; Scott et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is based on biochemical data and citations.

claim: K321A mutation weakens Vta1VSL binding to Vps4 hexamer 2-fold.
source: Consistent with the Vta1 surface electrostatic potential, point mutations K321A and R325D weaken Vta1VSL binding 2-fold and 3-fold, respectively, while E322A strengthens binding 2-fold.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence polarization binding data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: R325D mutation weakens Vta1VSL binding to Vps4 hexamer 3-fold.
source: Consistent with the Vta1 surface electrostatic potential, point mutations K321A and R325D weaken Vta1VSL binding 2-fold and 3-fold, respectively, while E322A strengthens binding 2-fold.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence polarization binding data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: E322A mutation strengthens Vta1VSL binding to Vps4 hexamer 2-fold.
source: Consistent with the Vta1 surface electrostatic potential, point mutations K321A and R325D weaken Vta1VSL binding 2-fold and 3-fold, respectively, while E322A strengthens binding 2-fold.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence polarization binding data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The effects of K321A, R325D, and E322A mutations on Vta1VSL binding are consistent with the Vta1 surface electrostatic potential.
source: Consistent with the Vta1 surface electrostatic potential, point mutations K321A and R325D weaken Vta1VSL binding 2-fold and 3-fold, respectively, while E322A strengthens binding 2-fold.
evidence: This is based on comparison of binding data with electrostatic potential calculations.

claim: Density accommodates the 8-residue ESCRT-III peptide in an extended conformation.
source: Density accommodates the 8-residue ESCRT-III peptide in an extended conformation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 6.

claim: The peptide density extends weakly at both ends and is not sufficiently clear to reliably build a model with side chains.
source: This density extends weakly at both ends and is not sufficiently clear to reliably build a model with side chains, consistent with the possibility that binding may occur in several overlapping positions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 6.

claim: The weak extension of peptide density at both ends is consistent with the possibility that binding may occur in several overlapping positions.
source: This density extends weakly at both ends and is not sufficiently clear to reliably build a model with side chains, consistent with the possibility that binding may occur in several overlapping positions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on the density characteristics.

claim: The primary contacts of the peptide are with pore loop 1 (residues 203–209) of the A, B, C, and D Vps4 subunits.
source: The primary contacts are with pore loop 1 (residues 203–209) of the A, B, C, and D Vps4 subunits, whose closest Cα atoms are ~7.5 Å from the helix axis that is defined by these loops.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the peptide-Vps4 interaction.

claim: The closest Cα atoms of pore loop 1 are ~7.5 Å from the helix axis.
source: The primary contacts are with pore loop 1 (residues 203–209) of the A, B, C, and D Vps4 subunits, whose closest Cα atoms are ~7.5 Å from the helix axis that is defined by these loops.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements.

claim: The peptide lies approximately along the helix axis, with Cα atoms modeled 1.0–2.7 Å (average 1.6 Å) from the axis.
source: The peptide lies approximately along the helix axis, with Cα atoms modeled 1.0–2.7 Å (average 1.6 Å) from the axis, which is consistent with the model that substrates are translocated along or close to the helix axis, with some variation allowed to accommodate distinct amino acid sequences.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements and modeling.

claim: The peptide position is consistent with the model that substrates are translocated along or close to the helix axis.
source: The peptide lies approximately along the helix axis, with Cα atoms modeled 1.0–2.7 Å (average 1.6 Å) from the axis, which is consistent with the model that substrates are translocated along or close to the helix axis, with some variation allowed to accommodate distinct amino acid sequences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The helical symmetry of pore loop 1 of Vps4 A-D has successive loops separated by a translation of 6.3 Å along the helix axis and a rotation of 60°.
source: The helical symmetry of pore loop 1 of Vps4 A-D is approximately continued by subunit E and has successive loops separated by a translation of 6.3 Å along the helix axis and a rotation of 60° (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The helical symmetry of pore loop 1 matches the translation and rotation seen every two residues along a canonical β-strand.
source: This matches the translation and rotation seen every two residues along a canonical β-strand, such that successive dipeptides of a β-strand that lies approximately along the helical axis could make equivalent interactions with pore loop 1 residues of successive Vps4 subunits.
evidence: This is based on comparison with known β-strand geometry.

claim: Successive dipeptides of a β-strand that lies approximately along the helical axis could make equivalent interactions with pore loop 1 residues of successive Vps4 subunits.
source: This matches the translation and rotation seen every two residues along a canonical β-strand, such that successive dipeptides of a β-strand that lies approximately along the helical axis could make equivalent interactions with pore loop 1 residues of successive Vps4 subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural symmetry match.

claim: Pore loop 1 residues of Vps4 A-D present a curved peptide-binding surface that extends into the hexamer pore.
source: Hence, these four loops present a curved peptide-binding surface that extends into the hexamer pore.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Pore loop 1 of subunit F is displaced ~14 Å from the helix axis and is completely disengaged from the substrate.
source: Pore loop 1 of subunit F is displaced ~14 Å from the helix axis and is therefore completely disengaged from the substrate (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Pore loop 2 residues of the Vps4 A-D subunits are arrayed contiguously with the pore loop 1 residues through the hexamer pore and follow the same helical symmetry.
source: Although we do not observe a contact between the peptide density and residues of Vps4 pore loop 2 (residues 241–251) and the density of pore loop 2 is generally quite poor, we note that these loops of the Vps4 A-D subunits are arrayed contiguously with the pore loop 1 residues through the hexamer pore and follow the same helical symmetry, which is consistent with the possibility that they continue the substrate binding surface used by Vps4 to translocate ESCRT-III subunits.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The arrangement of pore loop 2 is consistent with the possibility that it continues the substrate binding surface used by Vps4 to translocate ESCRT-III subunits.
source: Although we do not observe a contact between the peptide density and residues of Vps4 pore loop 2 (residues 241–251) and the density of pore loop 2 is generally quite poor, we note that these loops of the Vps4 A-D subunits are arrayed contiguously with the pore loop 1 residues through the hexamer pore and follow the same helical symmetry, which is consistent with the possibility that they continue the substrate binding surface used by Vps4 to translocate ESCRT-III subunits.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural arrangement.

claim: Vps4 translocates its ESCRT-III substrates through the hexamer pore by a helix propagation mechanism.
source: We propose that Vps4 translocates its ESCRT-III substrates through the hexamer pore by a helix propagation mechanism in which binding of ATP and Vta1 promotes growth at the A-end of the Vps4 helix while ATP hydrolysis and release promotes dissociation at the D/E-end of the helix (Figure 7B, Figure 8, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data.

claim: In the helix propagation mechanism, binding of ATP and Vta1 promotes growth at the A-end of the Vps4 helix.
source: We propose that Vps4 translocates its ESCRT-III substrates through the hexamer pore by a helix propagation mechanism in which binding of ATP and Vta1 promotes growth at the A-end of the Vps4 helix while ATP hydrolysis and release promotes dissociation at the D/E-end of the helix (Figure 7B, Figure 8, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data.

claim: In the helix propagation mechanism, ATP hydrolysis and release promotes dissociation at the D/E-end of the helix.
source: We propose that Vps4 translocates its ESCRT-III substrates through the hexamer pore by a helix propagation mechanism in which binding of ATP and Vta1 promotes growth at the A-end of the Vps4 helix while ATP hydrolysis and release promotes dissociation at the D/E-end of the helix (Figure 7B, Figure 8, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data.

claim: In repeated cycles, the propagating 4-subunit Vps4 helix will 'walk' along the substrate while binding it in an extended β-strand conformation.
source: In repeated cycles, the propagating 4-subunit Vps4 helix will 'walk' along the substrate while binding it in an extended β-strand conformation and conveying it through the hexamer pore.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data.

claim: The propagating Vps4 helix conveys the substrate through the hexamer pore.
source: In repeated cycles, the propagating 4-subunit Vps4 helix will 'walk' along the substrate while binding it in an extended β-strand conformation and conveying it through the hexamer pore.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the structural data.

claim: The overall effect of Vps4 translocation is expected to be unfolding of ESCRT-III structure as the Vps4 helix advances.
source: Some variation in strand conformation may be tolerated but the overall effect is expected to be unfolding of ESCRT-III structure as the Vps4 helix advances.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: Vta1 will promote the translocation process by binding adjacent Vps4 subunits in the helical conformation.
source: The structure indicates that Vta1 will promote this process by binding adjacent Vps4 subunits in the helical conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing Vta1 binding.

claim: Vta1VSL forms the same helix-promoting interaction between subunits F and A, as if pulling subunit F into an ATP-binding position at the leading end of the helix.
source: Moreover, as seen in the structure, Vta1VSL forms the same helix-promoting interaction between subunits F and A, as if pulling subunit F into an ATP-binding position at the leading end of the helix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: ATP hydrolysis correlates with expansion of the D-E nucleotide site to trigger disassembly of the helix.
source: At the other end of the helix, ATP hydrolysis correlates with expansion of the D-E nucleotide site to trigger disassembly of the helix, disengagement from the substrate by subunit F, opening of the interface to allow nucleotide exchange, and subsequent rebinding at the leading end of the propagating helix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing the expanded D-E interface.

claim: Each of the Vps4 subunits can make identical interactions with consecutive ESCRT-III dipeptides.
source: An attractive feature of this model is that the symmetry match between a β-strand ESCRT-III substrate and the pore loop 1 residues of the Vps4 helix means that each of the Vps4 subunits can make identical interactions with consecutive ESCRT-III dipeptides, and that these interactions do not need to change during the translocation process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the symmetry match between the substrate and pore loops.

claim: The interactions between Vps4 subunits and ESCRT-III dipeptides do not need to change during the translocation process.
source: An attractive feature of this model is that the symmetry match between a β-strand ESCRT-III substrate and the pore loop 1 residues of the Vps4 helix means that each of the Vps4 subunits can make identical interactions with consecutive ESCRT-III dipeptides, and that these interactions do not need to change during the translocation process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the symmetry match between the substrate and pore loops.

claim: The inherently weak hexamerization of Vps4 likely contributes to substrate specificity by coupling Vps4 recruitment to assembly of the active hexamer.
source: The inherently weak hexamerization of Vps4 (Monroe et al., 2014) likely contributes to substrate specificity by coupling Vps4 recruitment to assembly of the active hexamer.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known weak hexamerization and the proposed mechanism.

claim: Vps4 concentrates at ESCRT-III polymers by binding of its MIT domain with MIMs at the ESCRT-III C-termini.
source: As illustrated in Video 3, we envision that Vps4 concentrates at ESCRT-III polymers by binding of its MIT domain with MIMs at the ESCRT-III C-termini.
evidence: This is a model based on known MIT-MIM interactions.

claim: Vta1 possesses an N-terminal tandem MIT domain (t-MIT) that can bind MIM sequences.
source: Vta1 possesses an N-terminal tandem MIT domain (t-MIT) (Xiao et al., 2008) that can also bind MIM sequences and is connected to the VSL domain by a flexible ~100 residue linker.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: The Vta1 t-MIT domain is connected to the VSL domain by a flexible ~100 residue linker.
source: Vta1 possesses an N-terminal tandem MIT domain (t-MIT) (Xiao et al., 2008) that can also bind MIM sequences and is connected to the VSL domain by a flexible ~100 residue linker.
evidence: This is based on the Vta1 sequence and structure.

claim: The concentrating effect of Vps4 and Vta1 at ESCRT-III polymers is synergistic.
source: Because Vps4 and Vta1 also bind to each other, the concentrating effect at ESCRT-III polymers will be synergistic, and will promote Vps4 binding to ATP and hexamerization around the 30–170 flexible residues that lie between the MIM and the folded N-terminal domain of various ESCRT-III subunits (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple interactions between Vps4, Vta1, and ESCRT-III.

claim: The concentrating effect at ESCRT-III polymers will promote Vps4 binding to ATP and hexamerization.
source: Because Vps4 and Vta1 also bind to each other, the concentrating effect at ESCRT-III polymers will be synergistic, and will promote Vps4 binding to ATP and hexamerization around the 30–170 flexible residues that lie between the MIM and the folded N-terminal domain of various ESCRT-III subunits (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the avidity effect and known properties of Vps4.

claim: Various ESCRT-III subunits have 30–170 flexible residues that lie between the MIM and the folded N-terminal domain.
source: Because Vps4 and Vta1 also bind to each other, the concentrating effect at ESCRT-III polymers will be synergistic, and will promote Vps4 binding to ATP and hexamerization around the 30–170 flexible residues that lie between the MIM and the folded N-terminal domain of various ESCRT-III subunits (Han et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on known ESCRT-III structures and sequences.

claim: The Vps4 complex can hydrolyze ATP to translocate along the polypeptide until the ESCRT-III N-terminal domain is destabilized and removed from the polymer.
source: The Vps4 complex can subsequently hydrolyze ATP to translocate along the polypeptide until the ESCRT-III N-terminal domain is destabilized and removed from the polymer.
evidence: This is a model based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: If the polymer remains intact after removal of one subunit, Vps4 and Vta1 would remain at high concentration due to the continuing MIM-MIT interactions.
source: If the polymer remains intact after removal of one subunit, Vps4 and Vta1 would remain at high concentration due to the continuing MIM-MIT interactions and so could reassemble around another available ESCRT-III C-terminal sequence to repeat the process for as long as the ESCRT-III polymer persists to present an array of MIMs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The model that Vps4 translocates toward the N-terminal domain of ESCRT-III implies that substrate binds to the hexamer pore in a defined direction.
source: The model that Vps4 translocates toward the N-terminal domain of ESCRT-III implies that substrate binds to the hexamer pore in a defined direction, which is a level of detail that is not resolved in our current structure.
evidence: This is an inference from the proposed model and an acknowledgment of a limitation.

claim: The biological role of the 8-residue binding peptide identified from Vps2 is unresolved.
source: Also unresolved is the biological role of the 8-residue binding peptide that we identified from Vps2, which based upon structural information available for other ESCRT-III proteins likely corresponds to a short helix that packs against the folded core in an isolated ESCRT-III subunit (Bajorek et al., 2009; Xiao et al., 2009) and in an ESCRT-III polymer (McCullough et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of an unresolved question.

claim: The 8-residue peptide likely corresponds to a short helix that packs against the folded core in an isolated ESCRT-III subunit and in an ESCRT-III polymer.
source: Also unresolved is the biological role of the 8-residue binding peptide that we identified from Vps2, which based upon structural information available for other ESCRT-III proteins likely corresponds to a short helix that packs against the folded core in an isolated ESCRT-III subunit (Bajorek et al., 2009; Xiao et al., 2009) and in an ESCRT-III polymer (McCullough et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural information from other ESCRT-III proteins.

claim: The structures of Vps4 superimpose with other hexameric AAA ATPases, including the ATPases of the 26S proteasome.
source: The structure of Vps4 superimposes with other hexameric AAA ATPases, including the ATPases of the 26S proteasome, which, like Vps4, translocate protein substrates and adopt a right-handed helical notched-washer structure (Förster et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2016; Lander et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on structural comparisons shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ATPases of the 26S proteasome translocate protein substrates and adopt a right-handed helical notched-washer structure.
source: The structure of Vps4 superimposes with other hexameric AAA ATPases, including the ATPases of the 26S proteasome, which, like Vps4, translocate protein substrates and adopt a right-handed helical notched-washer structure (Förster et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2016; Lander et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on citations to proteasome structures.

claim: Multiple proteasome structures show four or five ATPase subunits forming a helix in which the pore loop 1 residues overlap Vps4 with RMSD values of ~2.3 Å.
source: Multiple proteasome structures show four or five ATPase subunits forming a helix in which the pore loop 1 residues overlap Vps4 with RMSD values of ~2.3 Å (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparisons shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ATP-bound conformation of the AAA ATPase NSF shows a similar overlap of pore loops to Vps4.
source: The ATP-bound conformation of the AAA ATPase NSF (Zhao et al., 2015) shows a similar overlap of pore loops (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), although the extent to which it may translocate substrate is unclear.
evidence: This is based on structural comparisons shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.
